articles.title: Balakot to Sindoor, India gave befitting reply: PM Modi on Pakistan terror
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a stern message to Pakistan, PM Modi said on Sunday the time when its role in sponsoring terror attacks on India would go unpunished is long
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a stern message to Pakistan, PM Modi said on Sunday the time when its role in sponsoring terror attacks on India would go unpunished is long gone, and his govt has made it clear with its actions, including Op Sindoor, that terrorists will be given a befitting response for their sinister designs against India.Modi's message came in his 'Mann ki Baat' broadcast as India marks the 10th anniversary of the surgical strikes on terror hideouts in Pakistan on Sept 28-29, 2016. "The world was astonished to see the manner in which our brave soldiers crossed the LoC to take action against terror. The strike demonstrated a new aspect of India's counter-terror policy. It was our decisive response to long-standing pain India had endured," he said."Over the past decade, from Balakot airstrike to Op Sindoor, India has repeatedly sent out a clear message: if terrorists dare to cast an evil eye on India, they will be met with a befitting response."'Zero-tolerance terror policy has borne results'Contrasting his government's targeted action against Pakistan to the approach of the previous Congress-led UPA govt, PM Narendra Modi said serial blasts had once become a common occurrence in the country. On Sept 13, 2008, serial blasts rocked Delhi and, just a few weeks later, the Mumbai terror attack stunned the country, the PM said.Demands for action against Pakistan following every terror attack used to be made then but were ignored. "Today, India pursues a zero-tolerance policy against terrorism, and we are witnessing the results of that," he said.During Op Sindoor, the Modi govt also unveiled a tougher national security doctrine, declaring that any future terror attack will be treated as an act of war. This eliminated the false distinction between terrorists and their state sponsors, it had said.Modi's message to Pakistan comes at a time when the nation is trying to airbrush its long association with terror incidents around the world, reflected in its PM Shehbaz Sharif's recent claims at the United Nations General Assembly about its role and sacrifices in combating terrorism.In his UNGA address, foreign minister S Jaishankar had snubbed Pakistan, calling it a "serial practitioner of terrorism" and asserting that India will continue to exercise its right to defend itself against terror threats.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: South African police discover body of 11th woman near Johannesburg
articles.summary: Police are investigating the killings in a country with one of the highest femicide rates in the world.
articles.body:
South African police have discovered the body of another woman east of the country’s commercial capital, Johannesburg, bringing the total number of female bodies found near the city since mid-July to 11.

Police said on Sunday that the latest victim was found in an open field in the Ekurhuleni municipality at about midday local time (10am GMT).

“A security company vehicle patrolling the area noticed the body and alerted the police,” police spokeswoman Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.

Details about the woman’s identity, age and cause of death were not immediately available.

Just one day earlier, on Saturday, the body of a semi-naked woman was found near a cemetery in the same municipality.

The latest discoveries add to growing concern over violence against women in a country long plagued by violent crime. While police work to establish whether the killings are connected, there have been community concerns that the murders are being carried out by the same killer or killers.

Provincial police chief Tommy Mthombeni said the victim found on Saturday appeared to have been stoned to death, but a post-mortem examination would be conducted to determine the cause of death.

Police said a man linked to the killing was arrested almost 400km (250 miles) away. His arrest brings the number of people in custody in connection with the series of killings to four.

President Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged the recovery of the body of the 10th victim while on the campaign trail for upcoming local elections, broadcaster eNCA reported.

“I’ve sadly heard about 10th body of a woman found in Thembisa,” Ramaphosa said on Saturday. “This continues to make us very sad, and in many ways, it’s a shame on the men of South Africa that we continue to kill the women of our beautiful country.”

South Africa has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, with an average of 15 women killed per day.

Two women have been charged with the murder of the woman whose body was the ninth discovered on September 17. Police have said the killing may have stemmed from a relationship-related matter.

Mthombeni, the provincial police chief, told state broadcaster SABC that investigators believe the ninth killing was an isolated case. However, he said it is possible some of the other killings are connected.

He added that some of the murders shared similarities, but cautioned that there is no conclusive evidence to suggest the same person or group is responsible.

Police discovered three bodies in July and August within 6km (4 miles) of one another in Ekurhuleni. Earlier this month, six bodies were found in 10 days, also in Ekurhuleni.

Prior to Saturday’s discovery, all of the deceased women were in their 20s or 30s. Several of them were found completely or partially naked.

The first body, discovered in mid-July, was found naked and restrained with cable ties. The victim’s boyfriend was subsequently arrested, but no charges were filed.

articles.title: Refugees in South Africa fear new attacks as September 30 deadline looms
articles.summary: Refugees in Durban say they have nowhere safe to return to after being forced from a makeshift camp.
articles.body:
Durban, South Africa – Bishop Raphael Bahebwa is in hiding, afraid he could be attacked for speaking out for the rights of foreigners in South Africa.

“I am in hiding now because they say they are going to kill me for speaking about the rights of foreigners,” he told Al Jazeera.

Bahebwa has lived in South Africa for 26 years, after arriving as a refugee from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

In that time, he has watched antiforeigner sentiment flare repeatedly in the country he came to call home. But he says this year feels different.

A September 30 deadline declared by March and March, an anti-immigration movement that has led protests across South Africa this year, has renewed fears of violence among migrant communities.

The group has called for undocumented foreign nationals to leave South Africa and has warned of further demonstrations if its demands are not met.

For Bahebwa and other refugees in Durban, however, the distinction between documented and undocumented migrants offers little comfort. They say the hostility they experience on the streets rarely begins with a request to see their papers.

South Africa will hold local government elections on November 4, in a campaign in which migration has become an increasingly prominent political and social issue.

For months, Bahebwa was among hundreds of refugees and asylum seekers who slept on the pavement outside the Durban Refugee Reception Centre on Che Guevara Road.

Many were from the DRC and Burundi, with others from Uganda, Mozambique and Tanzania. They said they had fled their communities because they feared antiforeigner attacks.

They arrived outside the Department of Home Affairs (DHA) office seeking safety.

Instead, the pavement became their home.

For roughly four months, men, women and children slept outside, exposed to the elements and dependent on civil society organisations and volunteers for food and other necessities.

“It has been very tough,” Bahebwa said. “Never before have I experienced something like this.”

Some of the migrants told Al Jazeera that conditions became desperate. They described irregular access to food and medication and said one man who had tuberculosis died while living at the camp. Al Jazeera has not independently established the circumstances of his death.

The camp was also not far removed from the hostility its residents said they had fled.

On September 3, members of March and March confronted refugees and asylum seekers living outside the centre. Violence broke out, and police intervened. At least four people were reported injured.

At another protest days later, police officers stood between the two groups, forming a barrier as tensions rose.

March and March has described its mobilisation as a campaign against undocumented immigration, crime and deteriorating conditions in South African communities.

The group says the government’s response to immigration enforcement has been insufficient.

Its leaders have repeatedly rejected accusations that their campaign is xenophobic and insist their target is undocumented migration rather than foreign nationals generally.

Bahebwa said documented and undocumented migrants alike have been caught in the hostility.

Earlier this year, six refugees working in salons around Durban’s Warwick Street Market were beaten by men carrying sticks, according to public-interest news outlet GroundUp. Two were hospitalised.

Bahebwa said the migrants had also struggled to obtain help from the authorities after earlier attacks.

“Police said we can’t open cases because we are foreigners. We had nowhere to go,” he alleged. Police have not publicly responded to that specific allegation.

In mid-September, the government moved to clear the makeshift camp outside the refugee centre.

The refugees were given a choice: return to the communities they had fled or accept temporary accommodation at the Lindela facility in Gauteng, hundreds of kilometres from Durban. Lindela is a government-run immigration detention facility used to hold people facing deportation.

Some feared going to Lindela, a facility historically associated with immigration detention and repatriation. Others felt they could no longer endure life on the pavement.

On September 15, 274 people were transported by bus from Durban to Lindela. About 150 others chose to remain in Durban and began trying to find alternative accommodation.

For those who stayed behind, leaving the pavement did not resolve the problem that had brought them there in the first place.

Kafuti Muyumba, a small business owner from the DRC and a representative of the refugee community, said many were afraid to return to neighbourhoods where they had built businesses and lives.

People are afraid, he said. “Even the police allow March and March violence. They came with sticks and say we are attacking them,” Muyumba told Al Jazeera.

He said many refugees had lost their livelihoods during the months of upheaval and were now desperate to find accommodation.

“This is not the first time we are experiencing xenophobia,” he said. “In 2008 and then in 2015 we also experienced this.”

In 2008, xenophobic violence spread through townships and informal settlements, killing dozens and displacing thousands.

Further outbreaks of violence against foreign nationals followed in subsequent years.

For Muyumba, those memories make the rhetoric surrounding September 30 difficult to dismiss.

“We don’t trust the police. They are not being fair with us. Some of them are also saying we must go,” he said.

Police have said there are no plans to change their normal policing approach because of the September 30 deadline and that any protesters will be expected to remain within the law.

March and March said all it wants is for undocumented immigrants to leave the country and return home.

But Muyumba said returning to the DRC is not a viable alternative for many Congolese refugees.

In response to ongoing protests, the South African government said it had intensified its immigration enforcement.

Between June 14 and August 20, authorities processed 86,596 foreign nationals for deportation and repatriation, according to the government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration.

Malawians made up the largest group, followed by Zimbabweans and Mozambicans.

Government data says 90 percent of those repatriated had entered South Africa illegally, while 95 percent were classified as having crossed the border outside official ports of entry.

The government says the operations form part of a broader effort to strengthen border management and enforce immigration law.

At the same time, officials have repeatedly warned private groups against taking immigration enforcement into their own hands.

March and March’s September 30 deadline has no legal authority. The government says common citizens cannot deport anyone from South Africa.

But deadlines do not need legal force to create fear, as was the case for an earlier deadline of June 30. For the refugees who spent months sleeping outside the DHA office in Durban, September 30 is another uncertainty layered on top of many others.

Some have been moved hundreds of kilometres away.

Others are trying to find new homes in the same communities they once fled. But among the migrants Al Jazeera spoke to, there is a shared anxiety that paperwork may offer limited protection when anger is directed first at being foreign.

Bahebwa has spent more than a quarter of a century in South Africa. For now, he says he is hiding and does not know what September 30 will bring.

“They are scapegoating us as foreigners,” he said. “It is not going to end on September 30. It has to do with the elections.”

Malawi migrants to South Africa line up for supplies at an informal refugee camp in Sherwood, Durban, South Africa, after fleeing their homes amid fears of xenophobic attacks [File: EPA]
Protesters hold placards during an anti-immigration march in Durban, South Africa, calling for tighter border controls and the deportation of undocumented migrants [File: Thuli Dlamini/Reuters]

articles.title: Foiled terror plot at bomber base signals wider threat to US military installations: expert
articles.summary: Five men arrested near RAF Fairford may have planned a complex, coordinated VBIED attack on U.S. strategic bombers, a former intelligence official says.
articles.body: Five men arrested near a key U.S. bomber base in the U.K. on Sunday may have planned a "complex," coordinated attack with potentially far-reaching security implications for American military installations globally, a former U.S. intelligence official warned. As counterterrorism police investigated after officers detained the suspects near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, a former Pentagon official also said President Donald Trump will ultimately be the one to decide the consequences if indeed the "trail leads to Tehran." The men were initially held on suspicion of offenses under Britain’s Explosives Act before being arrested on terrorism charges in connection with the airfield, a key U.S. Air Force hub and the primary European base for American strategic bombers. On Sunday, Trump said U.S. authorities had been monitoring the suspects prior to their capture. FORMER UK PRIME MINISTER TONY BLAIR WARNS EUROPE ‘WE DON’T WIN’ IN WAR WITHOUT US SUPPORT "We had them under investigation," Trump told reporters in Chicago. "They were looking to do big damage to our fort." "It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know. We worked with a lot of them. We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," Trump added. According to Sky News, counterterrorism police were investigating whether Iran is linked to the suspected bomb plot. Former Trump White House official Morgan Murphy told Fox News Digital that British authorities are leading the investigation alongside U.S. law enforcement and intelligence. "Every phone, bank record and rental receipt will be run through British and American intelligence, and if the trail leads to Tehran, it will be found," Murphy clarified. "But as American airmen and bombers seem to have been the target, Air Force investigators on the base, the FBI in London, and American intelligence will likely all work the case." "If conclusive evidence proves Iran is behind an attempted attack on U.S. forces, the American President will ultimately decide how Tehran pays," Murphy added. BRITAIN INTRODUCES SWEEPING NEW POWERS TO TARGET FOREIGN STATE-LINKED GROUPS INCLUDING IRAN'S IRGC Former Defense Intelligence Agency official Andrew Badger told Fox News Digital the number of suspects and vehicles involved raised the possibility of a sophisticated operation. "We are going to see elevated security protocols across Europe, across the U.K., and across the entire world for any U.S. installation," he said. "This is a very significant threat, and again, seeing that we had five individuals involved and three different reported vans at the scene, this could have been a very complex, highly orchestrated operation," Badger added. "This isn't just some type of amateur lone wolf operation," he said, noting Fairford’s strategic importance to the U.S. military. "Fairford is also where the U.S. houses its strategic bombers for Europe as well as the rest of the world." He said a potential attack posed broader risks beyond the airfield itself which he said "could have had significant security implications. It could have damaged the nearby area." HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY "They could have tried to use a VBIED or a vehicle-borne explosive device where the first van could have gone off at the front gate, and then the other vans would have gone in and tried to go for the strategic bombers," Badger said. British authorities have not publicly identified who they believe was behind the suspected plot or announced a motive, but RAF Fairford had taken on greater strategic importance during the war with Iran. The U.K. government previously authorized U.S. forces to use the Royal Air Force bases Fairford and Diego Garcia for limited defensive operations, including destroying Iranian missiles and launchers at their source. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later warned that any base used to attack Iranian territory would be considered a legitimate target. "Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory is a legitimate target for our forces," the IRGC said, according to reports. "Tehran warned London in July to keep American bombers off Fairford, and if this plot traces back to Iran, the answer must be more bombers, not fewer," Morgan said. IRAN EXPERT BRANDS ISLAMIC CENTER OF ENGLAND IRAN'S 'UK OFFICE,' URGES IMMEDIATE CLOSURE A local councilor told Reuters there had been a recent security alert at Fairford and surveillance had been stepped up. "So there was a specific threat about six weeks ago from the Iranians on this base. At the time, there was increased surveillance around the area," he told the outlet. Badger, however, cautioned against assuming Iran was responsible while pointing to other potential threats. "This could be Iran trying to gain strategic leverage in negotiations, but there are other actors as well," Badger added. "But there's Russia, who's been launching a campaign of gray zone or hybrid warfare attacks across Europe, as well as Islamic extremists, which are still a significant threat here in the U.K." "Was this some type of retaliation by Iran to perhaps try to gain leverage or to try to inflict a cost for the U.S. withdrawing from these negotiations? Again, we don't know for sure, but it is a possibility," Badger said. Badger also pointed to RAF Welford, a major U.S. ammunition storage facility that primarily supports operations at RAF Fairford. US EMBASSIES IN MIDDLE EAST WARN AMERICANS OF 'UNFORESEEN ESCALATION' AS LATEST STRIKES HIT IRAN "RAF Welford is actually the second-largest weapons and ammunition depot in all of Europe," Badger said, noting that the facility where the U.S. stores ammunition "could have been a target as well." "Other bases across Europe, including European and U.S. partners, have already been on a heightened state of alert," Badger continued. "But of course, after this attack, I think they're going to be in an even more heightened state. You're going to have more frequent security patrols." "There are reports that RAF Fairford was put onto what's called the Delta alert, which is the highest state of security alert within the military base system," Badger said. articles.title: Attorney for lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy mistrial pushes back on claims of refusing the law
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's holdout juror had "zero doubt" about his position, his attorney tells Kayleigh McEnany, citing "a mountain of evidence" for conviction.
articles.body: The attorney for the lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial is pushing back on a claim that his client refused to follow the law, telling Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany that the juror had no doubt about his decision. In a preview of an interview airing Monday on "Fox & Friends," McEnany asks attorney Edward Paltzik whether juror Michael P. Desronvil ever had reasonable doubt after the jury foreperson sent the judge a note accusing him of refusing to follow the law on reasonable doubt. "Michael had zero doubt," Paltzik says. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM "Zero doubt. No doubt. And he had evidence to back up his position?" McEnany responds. "A lot of evidence. A mountain of evidence," Paltzik says. LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR ADMITTED 'REASONABLE DOUBT' BUT STILL REFUSED INSANITY VERDICT, FOREPERSON SAYS Desronvil was the lone holdout after seven days of deliberations in Clancy’s trial. Eleven jurors were prepared to find the former labor and delivery nurse not criminally responsible for killing her three children, while Desronvil held out for a conviction. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4. Clancy admitted killing 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan at the family’s Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. Her defense argued that postpartum psychosis left her not criminally responsible. Prosecutors argued she understood what she was doing and planned the killings. LINDSAY CLANCY DA RARELY DOES PLEA DEALS, BUT HER CASE COULD BE THE 'EXCEPTION,' VETERAN ATTORNEY SAYS Desronvil later said he believed the physical evidence and witness testimony showed Clancy knew what she was doing. articles.title: Bacteria suspected in deaths of hundreds of baby whales off Argentina as calf deaths rise in Patagonia
articles.summary: A bacterial infection is suspected of causing the deaths of hundreds of southern right whale calves in Argentina’s Patagonia region, where dozens of dead
articles.body: A bacterial infection is suspected of causing the deaths of hundreds of southern right whale calves in Argentina’s Patagonia region, where dozens of dead young whales washed ashore again this week, continuing a trend that began in June. Researchers are investigating a possible outbreak of erysipelas, a serious bacterial disease commonly associated with bacteria found on the skin of the mammals. Scientists have not yet established the cause conclusively, while authorities continue working with researchers to investigate the deaths.Southern right whale calves continue washing ashoreDozens of dead southern right whale calves washed up on beaches in southern Chubut province again this week, continuing a pattern that began in June. Mariano Coscarella, a researcher at the Marine Mammals Laboratory of Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council (CONICET), told AFP that the mortality rate among young whales has been particularly high this season.The deaths are occurring in an important breeding area for southern right whales. Puerto Madryn and the nearby Valdes Peninsula are major breeding grounds for the species, which can grow up to 17 metres long and weigh about 40 tonnes.Researchers suspect a bacterial infectionVeterinarians suspect an outbreak of erysipelas, a serious disease caused by bacteria commonly found on the whales' skin. The Chubut provincial government said preliminary research indicated that the deaths may be linked to a “common marine bacteria” and that it was working with the scientific community to investigate what is happening.Coscarella said the deaths appeared to have a natural cause, while adding that the possible influence of human activity could not be completely ruled out. The suspected bacterial infection therefore remains part of an ongoing investigation rather than a confirmed explanation for all of the deaths.Nearly 400 calves counted dead this yearThe scale of the calf deaths comes as researchers continue monitoring the southern right whale population around Patagonia. AFP also reported that a record 2,110 whales were counted in the area in 2025, including about 800 young whales.This year, authorities have counted 1,375 whales, including nearly 400 calves, according to figures revealed by Coscarella. The figures come as researchers record an unusually high mortality rate among young whales during the current season.Scientists continue investigating the unusual number of deathsAuthorities in Chubut are working with scientists to determine what is causing the unusual number of deaths. While a bacterial disease is currently suspected, the investigation has not established that it is definitively responsible for all the whale deaths.Coscarella also said that the recent mortality does not constitute a medium-term danger to the area's whale population, noting the southern right whale's long lifespan. Local authorities estimate that the species can live for around 60 years.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: BASE jumper fatally plunges 700 feet after wingsuit failure in Utah
articles.summary: Authorities described the 27-year-old man, whose identity wasn’t released, as experienced in the endeavor.
articles.body: A 27-year-old BASE jumper died Sunday after his wingsuit failed when he launched from a 700-foot perch in Utah, authorities said. The man, whose identity was withheld until his family could be notified, fatally plunged from a mountainous area of Hyrum, Utah, east of Millville Canyon and east of the small city of Millville, Cache County Chief Sheriff’s Deputy Doyle Peck said. Search-and-rescue crews were called to Leetham’s Hollow, an area of canyon walls and cliffs not unlike the Grand Canyon’s, at 9:10 a.m. Sunday and declared the man dead at the scene, Peck said in a statement. “On today’s jump, something went wrong and he did not have enough lift with his wingsuit,” Peck said. “He impacted the ground at a high rate of speed resulting in his death.” The man was “experienced in this type of activity” and was part of a group of as many as 10 people who appeared to be engaged in wingsuit-aided BASE jumping, according to Peck. The area, about 45 miles north of Ogden, is popular with BASE jumpers, he said. A medical transport helicopter sent to help with the initial search transported the man’s body, Peck said. Before Sunday, 541 deaths around the world since 1981 had been logged by the BASE Fatality List, maintained by an online community for the sport. This year, 15 such deaths have been reported globally, according to the list. In June, two BASE jumpers died in a separate accident in Utah. One of them, Andy Lewis, performed onstage with Madonna at the 2012 Super Bowl. Photographer Carl Boenish helped coin BASE as a description of the sport’s adrenaline-inspiring launch points (buildings, antennas, spans, earth) in 1978, when he videotaped early jumps from Yosemite National Park’s El Capitan rock formation.

articles.title: Exceptional September warmth before rain returns this week
articles.summary: Temperatures remain above the average at the start of the week but wetter conditions are on the way for some
articles.body:
A vast area of low pressure in the Atlantic is set to draw warm south to south-easterly winds across the UK early this week, but for some rain will not be far behind.

Tuesday looks as if it will be the warmest day and after that temperatures will generally return closer to the September average.

Much of the UK can also expect a spell of wetter and windier weather from the approaching depression, with the most unsettled conditions likely to affect Scotland, Northern Ireland and western parts of England and Wales.

However, many central, southern and eastern areas of England, which have been affected by drought, may see far less rain.

Last week saw the autumn equinox, so our nights are now longer than our days.

This means that despite the warmth in the September sun, we are getting some cooler nights under clear skies.

So it will be notably chilly on Monday morning, perhaps with some fog patches to be aware of for the commute.

Once the fog clears a brighter day will follow for many, with high pressure allowing sunny spells and just a few scattered showers.

South-east England may see some welcome rain throughout the afternoon and evening, but it is by no means guaranteed. Temperatures will range from the mid to high teens, with some southern areas reaching 20C.

On Tuesday a strengthening southerly wind will bring a much warmer day.

Temperatures in the high teens are forecast in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and between 20 to 26 C for England and Wales.

However rain will move into Northern Ireland during the afternoon and then trek slowly eastwards throughout the evening and night. It may become persistent and occasionally heavy, with strong winds and gales for exposed coasts and hills.

Further east, drier and brighter conditions may remain before the rain arrives on Wednesday - it could possibly linger overnight.

Behind the rain it is back to sunny spells and scattered showers, and still windy in the west on Wednesday.

By Thursday, we are expecting high pressure to build, so it should be calmer and drier, and by Friday the north-west becomes the focus for any showers.

Of course the caveat is that forecast details may change, so you can stay up-to-date with the short term forecast for your area here .

Warmth continues but rain misses driest regions

Following the UK's hottest summer on record, September has been another notably warm month for many.

But it has also highlighted a stark north-west to south-east contrast.

While Scotland and other western areas have seen frequent Atlantic weather systems bearing rain and wind, much of central, southern and eastern England has remained largely dry with plenty of sunshine.

As a result, rainfall totals have varied dramatically.

Some drought-affected parts of England have received very little, while parts of north-west Scotland have been very wet.

Some parts - including Kirkwall and Prestwick - have already had nearly one-and-a-half times their average September rainfall. At Achnagart in the Highlands, rain has been recorded every day for the past 27 days.

Parts of Northern Ireland and Wales have had their average rainfall, whilst north-east England has seen some of the lowest amounts so far.

articles.title: Palestine Action protesters arrested outside UK Labour Party conference
articles.summary: Demonstrators protest against UK government’s proscription of Palestine Action as a ‘terrorist’ organisation.
articles.body:
Police in the United Kingdom have arrested more than 50 people protesting in support of the banned Palestine Action group outside a Labour Party conference in the northwestern English city of Liverpool.

The local Merseyside Police confirmed the arrests in a statement published on Sunday.

The police said those taken into custody at the protest, organised by Defend Our Juries, had displayed material in support of Palestine Action, proscribed as a “terrorist” group by the Labour government in July 2025 under the Terrorism Act.

According to the statement, police respected the rights of people to protest lawfully while aiming to keep the peace and ensure the public are safe.

More than 250 protesters sat outside the conference centre holding banners with words supporting the group on Sunday, before dozens of police began making arrests.

English band Massive Attack singer Robert Del Naja was among those arrested.

After asking demonstrators if they were going to continue holding up the signs, officers led people away, telling them they had been arrested under the Terrorism Act.

Reporting from Liverpool, Al Jazeera correspondent Milena Veselinovic said the protesters wanted to put proscription “front and centre of the UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s agenda” on the first day of his party’s annual conference.

“Being arrested is nothing in comparison to what the people in Gaza are going through, and it’s also worth it, because this is about our right to free speech,” one protester told Al Jazeera.

Another said that “there are priests, there are healthcare workers, there are people who deeply care, and deeply care about right and wrong.”

Kerry Moscogiuri, chief executive of Amnesty International UK, said protesting “is one of the most effective tools” to make government leaders listen and described the arrests as “a truly shameful attack on freedom of speech”.

“The new prime minister can reform our laws so that communities are protected in coming together and demonstrating on the issues they care about. Will he do so?” she said.

Activists also confronted Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband inside a restaurant in Liverpool, demanding that he lift the ban on the group and declare Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

The activists left after Miliband reportedly refused to comment.

A civil disobedience campaign has emerged since Palestine Action was outlawed in July 2025, with more than 3,600 people arrested for showing their support for the group, often while holding signs reading, “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.”

The UK Supreme Court is now set to hear the case after London’s Court of Appeal upheld the government ban in June.

articles.title: Venezuelans rally for opposition leader’s return and presidential elections
articles.summary: Nobel laureate Maria Corina Machado has been living in exile, with plans to return to Venezuela spoiled multiple times.
articles.body:
Hundreds of supporters of Venezuela’s opposition leader Maria Corina Machado have taken to the streets to demand her safe return and presidential elections that could lead to a democratic transition in the country.

In Caracas, hundreds of activists in sky blue shirts – the colour of Machado’s Vente Venezuela party – rode motorcycles through the capital’s main avenues on Sunday, honking their horns and waving Venezuelan flags. Similar demonstrations were held in state capitals, including Valencia, Maracaibo and Merida.

“This is not a matter of parties or politics,” said Flavio Valentini, a Vente Venezuela activist in Caracas who grabbed a megaphone and addressed the crowd. “This is a movement for the people and by the people.”

The weekend protests coincided with the return of Machado’s aide, Claudia Macero, to the country.

Macero, who ran press operations for Machado, returned from exile on Sunday to a cheering crowd at the airport serving Caracas.

“It is time to come home. It is time to recover the country,” Macero said as supporters sang the national anthem.

But she said that she did not yet know when Machado herself would be able to return.

“Maria Corina is trying every day to come home,” she said. “Evidently there is a very difficult process, but this will come to an end.”

Machado has been living in exile for the past nine months and has had plans to return to Venezuela spoiled multiple times. Opposition activists have accused Venezuela’s government of blocking her return, a claim the authorities deny.

Machado’s party said the opposition leader has made three unsuccessful attempts to return.

“We hope this transition process leads us to presidential elections and consolidates a free, democratic country that will be the main ally of the United States,” said Anthony Romero, a leader for Vente Venezuela, in Caracas.

The government has been widely accused of stealing elections, jailing dissidents and stifling freedom of speech. But late last week, Venezuela released more than three dozen political prisoners following a second round of talks backed by the US between the interim government and the opposition.

Machado, one of Venezuela’s most popular political leaders, was barred from running in Venezuela’s last presidential election by courts under the control of former President Nicolas Maduro. But her stand-in candidate is widely believed to have won the election with almost two-thirds of the vote.

Maduro claimed victory nevertheless and unleashed a violent crackdown against dissidents who protested the official results, forcing Machado and dozens of opposition leaders to go into hiding. Machado smuggled herself out of Venezuela last year after she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to restore democracy in the country.

US special forces abducted Maduro from his Caracas home in January, but Machado has been unable to return to Venezuela since then.

The government is now led by Delcy Rodriguez , a Maduro ally who has opened Venezuela’s oil industry to foreign investment and is working closely with the administration of US President Donald Trump.

Rodriguez told the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Wednesday that Venezuela would hold elections as part of a transition to “full democracy”, but did not give a date for the vote.

articles.title: Psychology says children need predictable boundaries more than constant freedom: How clear rules, consistency and choice help children develop self-control
articles.summary: A child asks for one more episode before bed. The parent says yes. Ten minutes later, the child asks for another.
articles.body: A child asks for one more episode before bed. The parent says yes. Ten minutes later, the child asks for another. The parent gives in again because it is late, everyone is tired and arguing feels harder than simply saying yes.The next evening, the same thing happens.For parents, these moments can look harmless. But over time, children are not only learning whether they can watch another episode. They are also learning whether rules mean what adults say they mean, whether expectations change depending on someone's mood and how much negotiation is needed before a limit disappears.This is where the idea of predictable boundaries becomes important.Child-development research does not suggest that children need parents who control every part of their lives. In fact, autonomy and age-appropriate independence are important for development. What children appear to benefit from is a combination of warmth, responsiveness, clear expectations and room to make choices.The distinction matters: predictable boundaries are not the same as rigid parenting.Children are still learning how to regulate themselvesSelf-regulation- the ability to manage emotions, attention and behaviour in pursuit of a goal- develops gradually. Young children cannot be expected to possess the same impulse control as adults because the skills required to pause, think and choose a response are still developing.The American Psychological Association describes childhood as a progression from co-regulation, where adults help children manage emotions and behaviour, towards self-regulation, where children increasingly do this themselves.That means a parent saying, "I know you want to keep playing, but it is bedtime. We can play again tomorrow," is doing more than enforcing a bedtime. The adult is providing an external structure while the child's internal ability to handle disappointment is still developing.Research has found links between parenting behaviours and the development of executive functions such as working memory and inhibitory control. A 2024 longitudinal study,(conducted at the University of Oregon, USA) following children from early childhood into adolescence found that greater parental autonomy support and supportive presence in early childhood were associated with stronger aspects of executive functioning in middle childhood, while greater parental hostility was associated with weaker inhibitory skills. In other words, children do not necessarily become self-regulated simply because adults stop regulating them.Sometimes they learn self-regulation because adults initially provide the structure they cannot yet provide for themselves.Predictability can make the world feel easier to navigateImagine being a child and not knowing what will happen when you break a rule.One day your parent laughs when you jump on the sofa. The next day they shout. On another day they ignore it. A rule may technically exist, but the child cannot predict its consequences.This is very different from: "We don't jump on the sofa. You can sit here or play on the floor."Research on household environments has repeatedly drawn attention to the role of predictability and organisation. A longitudinal study of 1,292 children found that household chaos and disorganisation in the early years were associated with later behavioural regulation, partly through their relationship with parenting and children's developing executive-function skills.Another study examining household chaos, parental responsiveness and children's executive functions highlighted the potential importance of structure, predictability and routines in children's cognitive development, while also noting that more research using causal designs is needed.The American Academy of Pediatrics similarly advises that children tend to do best when family routines are regular, predictable and consistent. At the same time, it cautions against making routines so rigid that children have little choice or flexibility.That balance is crucial.A boundary tells a child what to expect; control tells them they have no sayThere is a major difference between:"You have to be in bed by 9 pm because I said so" and "Bedtime is at 9 pm. You can choose whether you want to brush your teeth before or after putting on your pyjamas."Both provide a boundary. But the second gives the child some control within it. This approach resembles what psychologists call authoritative parenting- warmth and responsiveness combined with firm limits. The American Psychological Association describes authoritative parents as supportive and nurturing while maintaining clear limits, explaining rules and listening to the child's perspective without necessarily accepting every request.Freedom works better when children know where the edges areParents sometimes worry that saying no too often will make a child dependent, fearful or less confident. But freedom does not have to mean the absence of limits.A preschooler can choose between two outfits while still having a rule that they must get dressed before leaving for school. A school-age child can decide whether to do homework before or after an afternoon snack while knowing that homework needs to be completed before screen time. A teenager can have increasing freedom over friends, clothes and activities while still having agreed expectations around safety, communication and returning home.The boundaries change with age. In fact, good boundaries should become less restrictive as a child's capacity for responsible decision-making grows.The goal, therefore, is not to keep children inside an increasingly narrow box.It is to gradually make the box bigger as they become capable of handling more of the world themselves.Consistency matters more than having hundreds of rulesA predictable home does not need a rule for everything. In fact, too many rules can turn family life into a constant series of corrections. Instead, parents can identify a handful of non-negotiable boundaries around safety, sleep, respect, school responsibilities and family expectations. The important part is that adults respond to those boundaries with reasonable consistency.The AAP recommends clear and consistent rules, age-appropriate explanations and calm, predictable consequences rather than harsh punishment. It also encourages parents to listen to children and give them choices among acceptable alternatives.This can sound surprisingly ordinary:"We don't hit. You can tell me you're angry.""Screen time is finished for today. You can be upset about it.""You need to wear a helmet if you want to ride the bicycle.""You can choose the blue cup or the red one."These sentences do something powerful: they allow the child's feelings to exist without allowing those feelings to decide every boundary.And parents do not have to be perfectly consistentReal families are messy. Parents get tired. Work runs late. Festivals disrupt bedtime. Travel changes routines. Grandparents may have different rules. Sometimes a parent says yes when they meant no. Predictability is not perfection.The aim is to create enough consistency that children generally understand how their world works - and enough flexibility that they can learn to cope when it doesn't.The American Academy of Pediatrics itself describes healthy routines as a balance between the chaos that can come without structure and the boredom or inflexibility that can come from excessive rigidity.That may be the most useful way for parents to think about boundaries.Children do not need every minute planned. They need to know that someone is paying attention, that certain rules will hold, that their feelings will be heard and that they have some choices within the framework.The eventual goal of boundaries is not obedience for its own sake. It is to help children gradually develop the ability to set boundaries for themselves.Today, a parent says, "It's time to stop playing."Over time, the child learns to notice, "I have school tomorrow, so I should probably stop playing now."That shift- from an external rule to an internal decision- is where predictable boundaries can become something much more valuable than discipline: the foundation for independence.You use AI every day. articles.title: September 28, 1066: 'William the Conqueror' reached England; how he reshaped country's land ownership system
articles.summary: On September 28, 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, landed at Pevensey in southern England with an invasion force of around 7,000 men, including 2,000-3,000
articles.body: On September 28, 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, landed at Pevensey in southern England with an invasion force of around 7,000 men, including 2,000-3,000 cavalry. His arrival marked the beginning of the final phase of his bid for the English throne, but it was his subsequent conquest and consolidation of power that transformed the ownership and administration of land across England.William defeated King Harold II at the Battle of Senlac, near Hastings, on October 14. He was crowned King of England on Christmas Day 1066.The conquest was followed by a major redistribution of land. According to the Royal Family's account of William I, his wholesale confiscation of land from English nobles and their heirs allowed him to grant land tenancy to Norman, French and Flemish allies in return for military service.William transferred land from nobles who had not supported him to Norman barons who had backed his conquest. The resulting feudal structure placed the king at the top: large areas of land were granted to barons, who in turn granted portions to knights, while peasants worked the land and paid taxes and provided produce.The shift was substantial. By the end of William's reign, a small group of the king's tenants had acquired about half of England's landed wealth, while only two Englishmen still held large estates directly from the king, according to the Royal Family.William also created up to 180 'honours' - estates scattered across different shires, generally centred on a castle. By the end of his reign, more than 80 castles had been built across England.The Domesday BookThe redistribution of land also created a practical problem for William: he needed to know who held land and how much wealth it represented.The cost of his military campaigns, defence measures and the devastation in northern England prompted a detailed investigation into the kingdom's land and wealth. The result was the Domesday survey of 1086 and the two-volume Domesday Book.The Domesday Book as a detailed survey of land, wealth and life in medieval England. Commissioners recorded who owned land, its value, the people living and working on it, woodland, animals and buildings, as well as the value of land and goods in 1066 and 1086.The survey provided a record that could be used for taxation and administration. According to BBC Bitesize, the Domesday Book recorded more than 13,000 places across England.Its figures also show the scale of the post-Conquest shift in landholding. William directly controlled about 20 per cent of the land, Norman nobility controlled about 50 per cent, the Church about 25 per cent, and English nobility about 5 per cent.The Royal Family states that the survey was also linked to William's need to maximise tax revenues and establish the direct loyalty of his feudal tenants. In 1086, his 170 tenants-in-chief and other important landowners gathered for the Oath of Salisbury and swore fealty to him.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: ‘Storm fatigue’: Hawaiians reeling from back-to-back hurricanes as Nolo’s threats diminish
articles.summary: A hurricane watch was in effect for the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, which Nolo was expected to approach Tuesday,
articles.body: HILO, Hawaii — Hawaiians have storm fatigue, Hilo’s mayor said Sunday, as the third hurricane to approach the islands in recent weeks continues to spin offshore. The relatively calm state has been battered by the effects of multiple hurricanes, including Lala, Lowell and now Nolo, as the eastern and central Pacific have churned out at least 19 named storms. None of the three hurricanes has made landfall in Hawaii. “So there’s storm fatigue and there’s some PTSD,” Mayor Kimo Alameda told NBC News on Sunday. “I mean, you know, there’s a lot of anxiety around the weather now. You know, a lot of our folks out in the south side, they experienced, you know, catastrophic flooding,” he said, referring to the impacts of Hurricane Lala last month. That storm killed two people, Alameda said, and damaged more than 200 homes without making landfall. Gov. Josh Green subsequently issued three disaster proclamations related to damage from separate storms in September alone. Officials have reported some rescues but no deaths or major damage from Nolo. “We did take some hits in some parts of the island,” Alameda said. “For the most part, we dodged a huge bullet. It could have been much worse.” More than 120 National Guard members were activated on the island for Nolo, among roughly 400 statewide, after Green issued an emergency proclamation. President Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate assistance and provide funding support. In Nāʻālehu, at the island’s southern point, Peggy McKibbin surveyed silt-covered roads from her four-wheeler Sunday and pointed out the lingering damage from Lala — a bakery, a fire station and a hardware store wiped out. “Everyone has been very much affected by this,” McKibbin said. Nolo was a Category 4 major hurricane Sunday afternoon and forecast to strengthen, but the center was expected to remain south and southwest of the Hawaiian Islands. A hurricane watch was in effect for the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, which the storm was expected to approach Tuesday, according to the National Hurricane Center. The Pacific has been unusually active this season, according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec, with storm activity running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. He said the pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often gets more tropical storms and hurricanes. Alameda, Hilo’s mayor, said people are ready if another hurricane comes their way. “Unfortunately, we’ve been having a lot of practice,” he said, noting a recent tsunami threat and earthquake, as well as a precautionary eye on the volcano Kīlauea. Mexico’s Baja Peninsula, meanwhile, was bracing for the arrival of major Hurricane Polo on Monday after it lashed parts of the country’s southwest coast with rain and strong winds. Polo remained a dangerous Category 3 storm with top sustained winds of 125 mph, the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said Sunday afternoon. Polo was moving to the north-northwest at 12 mph about 285 miles west-southwest of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, according to the hurricane center. The Mexican navy said in a statement that it had gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlán, on the Pacific Coast, and deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the hurricane. Also Sunday, Tropical Storm Rachel formed off Mexico’s southwest coast. Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and was about 275 miles south of Acapulco. A tropical storm watch was in effect. Ryan Chandler, Shanshan Dong and The Associated Press reported from Hilo and Dennis Romero from San Diego.

articles.title: Australia could run its electricity grid without fossil gas at similar cost; researchers say models underestimate long-duration storage
articles.summary: Researchers at the Australian National University, led by Timothy Weber, have found that Australia's electricity system could be run without any fossil
articles.body: Researchers at the Australian National University, led by Timothy Weber, have found that Australia's electricity system could be run without any fossil gas at essentially the same cost as a gas-dependent grid, in a study ‘Replacing gas with low-cost, abundant long-duration pumped hydro in electricity systems’ published in Cell Reports Physical Science. The team argues that many long-term energy plans, including Australia's own, can be biased towards gas because of the way their models simplify decades of weather and demand data, combined with outdated assumptions about how much pumped hydro storage costs and how much can be built. Here's how the researchers uncovered the bias, and what fixing it means for the country's energy future.Why energy models keep concluding Australia needs gasTo manage the huge computing demands of modelling decades of hourly data, most long-term energy plans compress that data using "temporal aggregation" techniques, shortcuts that reduce complexity but can distort the picture of how storage actually behaves. The researchers tested four such techniques on a modified version of the Australian Energy Market Operator's 2024 Integrated System Plan model, finding that three of them badly underestimated the value of long-duration storage, some capturing only daily cycling and missing seasonal patterns entirely. Only one method, based on "segmentation," closely matched a full, unsimplified simulation, showing that flawed shortcuts, not physical reality, were steering models toward gas.Fixing the flawed pumped hydro assumptionsThe researchers found that institutional energy plans often overlook off-river pumped hydro by imposing restrictive build limits, short storage durations and relatively high capital costs. A global pumped hydro atlas identified about 818,000 off-river sites worldwide, with a combined storage potential of 86 million GWh outside protected areas and large urban centres. For Australia's National Electricity Market, the atlas identified about 287,000 GWh of technical storage potential across the NEM states, including 200 premium-cost sites in southeastern mainland Australia comparable with or better than sites considered in Tasmania.By contrast, none of the 17 energy plans examined allowed new pumped hydro with storage durations longer than 48 hours. The researchers found that, after applying lower-cost assumptions, relaxing build limits and adding a 160-hour pumped hydro option, the model selected much longer-duration storage, with the 100% renewable scenario building about 1,200 GWh of new pumped hydro with an average duration of 75 hours.What a 100% renewable grid actually costsOnce the researchers corrected these pumped hydro assumptions and used the more accurate segmentation modelling method, a fully renewable grid for Australia's National Electricity Market came out costing about the same as a gas-dependent one, built around roughly 1,200 gigawatt-hours of new pumped hydro storage. Achieving this also required a fairly modest amount of extra solar and wind capacity, on average just 670 megawatts of solar and 370 megawatts of wind more per year than a system that kept relying on gas, a small fraction of what Australia already installs annually. The researchers estimate Australia's current pumped hydro development pipeline sits at only around 192 gigawatt-hours, far short of what would be needed.Why batteries alone can't replace long-duration storageThe study is careful to note that batteries and pumped hydro aren't competitors so much as partners suited to different jobs. Batteries remain excellent for short bursts of high-power storage, but scaling them up to replace 1,200 gigawatt-hours of long-duration storage would cost an estimated six to twelve times more than pumped hydro, adding roughly US$17 to 20 billion a year in extra costs. Together, the researchers found, pumped hydro and batteries can already provide the same frequency control, voltage control and backup services that gas generators offer. The researchers also note that batteries already supply 66% of frequency control ancillary services in Australia's National Electricity Market, compared with 11% from hydro and less than 1% from gas.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Unacceptable cynical attempt': Why US rejected Iran's ceasefire proposal
articles.summary: US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said on Sunday that Washington rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz because Tehran
articles.body: US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said on Sunday that Washington rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz because Tehran sought sanctions relief and access to “billions in frozen assets” before talks on its nuclear programme.“They were asking for everything up front, with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on CNN’s “State of the Union” when asked what US President Donald Trump objected to.In a separate interview with NBC, Waltz called Iran’s proposal “a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable.” He said the US would ultimately need to reach “some type of agreement” with Iran, while stressing that Trump would keep all “options on the table”.Waltz said Iran’s seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz included a “request to have access to billions in frozen funds and a request for the lifting of sanctions”.“These aren’t just the United States’s sanctions,” Waltz said. “These are global sanctions. It’s worth reminding people that this is the world’s position.”Waltz also pointed to Iran’s nuclear programme, saying that “there has been not one, not two, but seven UN Security Council resolutions over the last 20 years saying Iran cannot and should not have a nuclear weapons programme”.He added that the International Atomic Energy Agency had referred Iran to the Security Council “for violations”, including Tehran’s refusal to allow inspectors into the country and provide “proper oversight of their enrichment”.Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi later disputed Waltz’s account of the proposal.“I am surprised that the ambassador is talking about a seven-day plan, as he has not read it,” Araghchi said. “Maybe he has not been given a copy.”However, Araghchi has also said Iran remained open to diplomacy while warning that Tehran was prepared for renewed hostilities.“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed. We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war. We don’t care about U.S. midterm elections. We care about our national interests. At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose,” he said.US President Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s seven-day ceasefire proposal and told aides he expects US bombing of Iran to resume after the November midterm elections, according to US officials cited by The Washington Post.Under Tehran’s proposal, the US would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, ease sanctions on Iranian oil exports and observe a ceasefire that would include Lebanon. In return, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations with Washington on its nuclear programme.Trump has said Tehran is seeking a deal after the midterm elections that would dismantle its nuclear programme. However, according to The Washington Post, he remains privately skeptical that Iran would meet his demands and has told aides that renewed bombing is likely.However, Trump expressed confidence that the conflict with Iran would be won “very soon”, while acknowledging that fresh US military strikes before the November midterm elections were “possible”.Speaking to Fox News on the sidelines of the PGA Tour Presidents Cup on Sunday (local time), Trump said an end to the confrontation would lead to a sharp fall in global oil prices. He reiterated that preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon remained the primary US objective.“I think what's going to happen is we're going to win this war very soon, and as soon as we win it, the oil will go down, way down to what it was before the war,” Trump told Fox News.With Iran maintaining its position despite Trump’s threat of further military action and rejection of its peace proposal, tensions in West Asia could intensify after the US midterm elections.You use AI every day. articles.title: Over 200 melted road reports in East of England over four years
articles.summary: Experts warn England's roads are built for cold weather rather than heatwaves.
articles.body:
The number of cases of roads melting in the East of England has risen by 67% in the past three years, data obtained by the BBC shows.

The region's highways authorities reported more than 200 cases of melting roads in the past four years, following the BBC's request for information.

Experts said that part of the problem was caused by most UK roads being designed for cooler weather rather than prolonged periods of "extreme heat".

The Department for Transport (DfT) said it was supporting local highway authorities to improve the resilience of road networks through guidance, tools and resources.

Earlier this year the A143 at Stanton, near Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, was shut as an emergency measure amid reports patches of asphalt were being lifted up by cars using the road.

It was the second time this year the road surface was reported to have melted as a result of high temperatures.

But the BBC, which asked all highways authorities in the East of England how many instances of roads melted by hot weather they had dealt with in each financial year since 2023, has now established the Stanton incident was merely one of dozens across the region.

What can this pothole tell us about the state of UK roads?

Why are our roads melting – and what can be done?

According to comparable figures from eight authorities, the number of melted road cases rose from 33 in 2023-24 to 55 in 2025-26.

In Suffolk instances of melting roads rose from three cases to eight and in Norfolk the number of "dustings" - when gritting lorries spread light dustings of sand or stone to prevent road tarmac from melting - rose from 29 to 46.

Buckinghamshire Council did not provide data for the 2023-24 to 2025-26 but said it had received 59 cases since April this year.

Essex had one incident in both 2024-25 and 2025-26 and a further six cases since April this year.

West Northamptonshire Council said it had two incidents in the past three years while North Northamptonshire Council said it did not hold data about melted roads.

Cambridgeshire, Hertfordshire, Thurrock councils said they had not experienced any incidents with melting roads in the past three years.

As well as the Stanton cases, Suffolk County Council said it had a further eight incidents this summer.

A spokesman for the authority said: "While incidents of roads being affected by hot weather remain relatively uncommon, Suffolk Highways has experienced a small number of cases following periods of exceptionally high and prolonged temperatures."

The council said it used granite dust during periods of "extreme heat" and said it "continues to work with other local highway authorities, industry partners and suppliers to explore innovative maintenance techniques and materials that improve network resilience".

This work includes looking at new road treatments that can withstand a wider range of temperatures.

"Through ongoing research, trials and sector-led collaboration, the highways industry is continuing to develop and identify best practice solutions that will help ensure the long-term resilience and performance of highway assets," the spokesman said.

Dr Mashael Kamran is a post-doctoral research associate at the University of Cambridge whose work looks at the future building and maintenance of the country's transport infrastructure.

"Many of our roads were built for the cooler winter weather rather than the warmer weather we are seeing," she said. "When air temperatures reach 30C (86F), the roads below can go up to 50C (122F). On top of that, when you've got heavy duty traffic as well, that can cause rutting of the roads."

She said tight council budgets meant many authorities were increasingly surface dressing or patch repairing roads rather than relaying them, which meant they remained susceptible to melting in hot weather.

"That doesn't really help in a heatwave situation," she said.

She said part of her work involves exploring various road materials that perform at a wider range of temperatures and how to prioritise where limited budgets are spent first.

The Chartered Institute for Highways and Transportation (CIHT) said high temperatures were having a "significant impact" on roads.

It said when air temperatures are 30C the road surface can reach between 40C and 50C adding that some roads start to soften above 50C.

Sue Percy, the chief executive of CIHT, said: "Climate disruption is no longer a future challenge.

"Highway authorities and transport operators are already seeing the effects of higher temperatures and more extreme weather on the transport network.

"When transport networks are disrupted by extreme heat, the consequences go beyond damaged infrastructure. Communities can lose access to jobs and essential services, businesses face delays and disruption, and the wider economy suffers."

A spokesperson for the DfT said: "We recognise the impact of extreme heat on our road network, which is why we are investing a record £7.3bn in local highway maintenance, and working closely with local authorities to help manage the impacts of hot weather on roads."

articles.title: Department of Labor IG Anthony D'Esposito hints at 'total shutdown' of H-1B via program; says: 365 days from now ...
articles.summary: Anthony D’Esposito, Inspector General at the Department of Labor, has hinted at a potential “total shutdown” of the H‑1B visa program within the next year.
articles.body: Anthony D’Esposito, Inspector General at the Department of Labor, has hinted at a potential “total shutdown” of the H‑1B visa program within the next year. Speaking in Washington, D’Esposito said investigators are building a sweeping case against fraud in the foreign labor system, adding: “We have handcuffs ready… We are building a case. I think that the efforts and the focus that you see from the White House and from this administration is telling a story. We are laying out the case very vividly to the American people. l think that the foreign labor visa program is going to look very different 365 days from now than it does today."The remarks come amid an aggressive push by the Trump administration to tighten oversight of the H‑1B program, which allows U.S. employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations.What Department of Labor IG Anthony D'Esposito said about H-1B visaIn an interview with commentator Benny Johnson, D'Esposito warned that the H-1B program could look "very different" a year from now as the Trump administration steps up investigations into alleged foreign-labour fraud. Some outlets read his remarks as pointing to a total shutdown of the program, though his own words were that the system will look very different in 365 days. He also said his team has "handcuffs ready" for offenders.He described the effort as a deliberate, public case-building exercise. "We are laying out the case very vividly to the American people," he said, adding that the White House's focus tells its own story. He rejected the idea that this is routine compliance work, saying it is not a paperwork accounting issue and that "this is real."A widening investigationAccording to reports, the administration is expanding a nationwide investigation into alleged foreign labor fraud, worker exploitation and potential human trafficking. In a separate post, D'Esposito referred to alleged "fake employers," "sham jobs" and "visa mills," and the Labor Department's Office of Inspector General said on September 18 that it had issued dozens of subpoenas and executed search warrants in multiple locations.The office is also looking beyond H-1B. In a September 22 post, D'Esposito said his office is targeting colleges accused of exploiting J-1 visas, following the sponsors, grant money and people behind the scheme, and told fraudsters to expect cuffs.The policy backdropThe enforcement push runs alongside other administration measures. A presidential executive order now requires federal agencies to assess whether employers seeking foreign petitions have recently laid off similarly situated American workers, and the administration has introduced a $100,000 fee for certain new offshore petitions, along with extended entry restrictions on some overseas H-1B recipients through September 2027. The White House has said the earlier restriction was followed by a 92 per cent decline in H-1B registrations from the largest US IT outsourcing firms.The Labor Department also launched a related enforcement effort last year. In September 2025 it announced Project Firewall, aimed at ensuring employers prioritize qualified Americans in hiring and holding them accountable for abusing the H-1B process.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tech firm Halo moves into Ipswich's landmark Willis building
articles.summary: Halo moves into the Willis Building on Monday with ambitions to create 5,000 jobs in 10 years.
articles.body:
The founder of a technology company says its move to the heart of Ipswich will help make the town a "start-up incubator" that will keep young talent in the county.

Halo is moving its headquarters to the Willis Building - a Grade I listed glass office space designed by Lord Norman Foster, with insurance firm Willis - now called WTW - retaining a smaller presence there.

Founder Paul Hamilton confirmed to the BBC that staff will move into the building on Monday - and 250 people will be based there by the end of the year.

"This move reinstates our commitment to the region, and ambition to make Ipswich a tech hub," he said, adding that the firm wanted "to respect a historic and iconic building".

He says the company has ambitions to "create 5,000 jobs in 10 years".

It celebrated its 50th anniversary last year after being originally built for the insurance firm.

Worth an estimated £1bn, Halo is a global software company that builds IT service management and workflow platforms, used by major organisations such as Microsoft and Red Bull.

The company focuses its recruitment on graduates - with the average employee age about 24.2 years.

Hamilton said the move to the Willis Building was a "huge next step" and gave the company "the capability to expand further and hit our target of 1,000 graduates in Ipswich by the end of 2030".

"We are looking forward to working alongside WTW after the incredible 50 years they've had in the building so far," he said.

Halo initially had two offices in Stowmarket but will keep one open.

Last year, the software firm replaced Ed Sheeran as the main sponsor of Ipswich Town's football shirts .

Jack Abbott, Labour MP for Ipswich, previously said the move was "massive" for the town, and that it symbolised "our economic rejuvenation".
