articles.title: Thousands of illegal ghost plates on cars revealed by new cameras
articles.summary: Illegal registration plates are far too easy to get hold of and are putting the public at risk, BBC is told.
articles.body:
Thousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal.

These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones, as well as track criminals.

Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor.

We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved.

Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks.

The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it.

The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition.

These tactics include deliberately using false plates that clone the number of another vehicle - and so-called "ghost plates", where special plastic is used to make all or part of the registration number unreadable by most motorway cameras.

One of the main providers of ANPR technology, MAV Systems, has been testing a new camera capable of identifying and reading ghost plates.

At one test site, just outside London near the Dartford Crossing, it has recorded an average of more than 1,000 of the ghost plates a day over several months.

Two other sites have been running for almost two years. At one, near the M25, detections have risen from 1,000 a day to nearly 2,000 a day - while at the other, near the Eurotunnel at Folkestone, the system is flagging more than 400 a day.

Sharon Gannon's son, Jason Wallis, died in a crash where hidden registration plates were involved. She believes being invisible to ANPR cameras emboldens drivers to take deadly risks.

Wallis was killed in Buckinghamshire in 2023. He and his brother-in-law, Lewis Baker, had been riding their motorbikes at high speed when they both crashed into a car. The car driver was not hurt.

Baker survived and was later jailed for 15 months for dangerous driving . In court, he admitted using a device to hide his number plate from public view. He also said he and Wallis had ridden at high speed more than 100 times.

"It has broken us all," Sharon Gannon says of the effect the crash has had on her family.

In another case, from 2025, 81-year-old Graham Slinn was killed on a pedestrian crossing when a car with cloned plates hit him at high speed.

The 20-year-old driver, Cain Byrne, who was driving without a licence or insurance, had also inhaled nitrous oxide minutes before the collision. He was identified after police trawled through hours of CCTV footage. One camera even caught the moment he had put the illegal plates on his car.

Byrne was jailed for 11 years and six months for causing death by dangerous driving, driving while disqualified and driving without insurance.

The victim's daughter, Nicola Timmis, says cloned plates are like a "gateway drug" which allow drivers to take more dangerous risks.

"It seems like it's harmless, but then one thing leads to another, leads to another, and before you know it, it's somebody dead," she tells Panorama. "It is not a victimless crime."

Both cloned and ghost plates look like normal vehicle registration plates when viewed by the naked eye.

In the case of cloned ones, at least two vehicles are on the road with the same letters and numbers - with only one of them being legal.

Ghost plates, on the other hand, show correct details for the vehicle - but they are made up of reflective materials which are difficult or impossible for most ANPR cameras to read.

Cloned and ghost plates undermine the police's ability to track organised criminals, says Tony Porter, a former senior counter-terrorism officer who has advised the government on surveillance cameras.

"The police need an effective ANPR system that doesn't have weaknesses [and] doesn't put the public at risk," he says.

While passports have security features such as watermarks and electronic ID chips, Porter says, "we tolerate a £10 number plate with no security mechanism on it".

In the UK, there are more than 34,000 businesses registered with the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) to supply number plates.

Anyone can currently become a registered number-plate supplier by filling in a quick form and paying a one-off fee.

Panorama secretly filmed at a market in Essex to find out how easy it is to buy a plate in breach of the rules.

Two out of three businesses we approached there offered ghost plates which they said could help avoid cameras policing London's Ultra-Low Emission Zone (Ulez) cameras.

One of them allowed us to buy a plate without asking for either ID or proof that we were allowed to use the registration - both of which are required by law.

Instead, we handed over £40 in cash and, eight minutes later, we had a brand new number plate. Buying a ghost plate is not illegal in itself, but it would be against the law to put it on a vehicle and drive with it.

Just two number plate suppliers have been prosecuted and forcibly removed from the DVLA register since 2020, a Freedom of Information request by Panorama has discovered. Only six DVLA officers are tasked with inspecting and auditing the thousands of registered suppliers in the UK.

The DVLA said in a statement that it was "cleaning up the register, strengthening compliance and enforcement" and that it continued to work closely with police and Trading Standards to "tackle suppliers who break the rules".

To witness the scale of the problem, Panorama joined the police and DVLA at a location on the edge of Birmingham and West Bromwich to see a roadside operation checking for illegal number plates and other issues.

Not long after we arrived, officers stopped a van. Specialist infrared goggles - which see number plates the way ANPR cameras do - revealed it was displaying a ghost plate. The driver received a £100 fine but said he was unaware the plate was illegal.

The police and DVLA then visited the plate supplier, where staff denied selling ghost plates. But, using the goggles to view the supplier's stock, Panorama identified two ghost plates displayed on a wall alongside several legal ones.

Police also discovered the supplier kept ghost letters and numbers separately on a shelf, which they said suggested "some level of intent".

The supplier, which told Panorama it did not manufacture the letters it used to make plates, received a warning letter, although a prosecution is still being considered.

Police forces want to see tighter licensing and regulation around who can issue a number plate, says Chief Constable Tim Forber, the UK's policing lead on ANPR.

"Not a week goes by where we don't see an example of someone on cloned plates involved in serious and organised crime," he adds.

There is a problem that needs tackling and a more robust system may be needed, according to Justin Madders, the minister in charge of UK vehicle registration.

He says the government recognises this and is creating a national centre to crack down on illegal number plates, bringing together police forces to share intelligence and trial new technologies to improve road safety, tackle organised crime and drivers attempting to dodge fines.

"I don't think we can rule anything in or out at this stage," he adds.

articles.title: Getting River Avon pollution investigated like 'pulling teeth'
articles.summary: Bristol residents say an oil-like substance has been bubbling up for years and killing wildlife.
articles.body:
An oil-like substance has been bubbling up in the River Avon in Bristol for years and killing wildlife, according to local residents who have made regular reports to the Environment Agency (EA).

Nicola Irvine, who lives in Crews Hole, said it had been like "pulling teeth" getting the EA to investigate the pollution since she contacted them in July 2025.

Her partner, Toby White, said: "It's hard to describe how bad the smell is - at times it's like you're living on a petrol station and you start getting headaches."

The EA said it had already visited the site and was "continuing to investigate the source of contamination and its damage to the environment".

An EA spokesperson added: "While minor impacts have been found where the contamination has entered the watercourse, we have not found wider environmental effects downstream.

"We continue to work with landowners, the local authority and partner organisations to take action to protect the local environment."

'Batch cooking saves my family of eight a fortune'

Why saunas are becoming the new dating hotspot

Nearby is a popular swimming spot at Conham River Park where there has been years of campaigning to protect the Avon from pollution, most recently with a charter of rights for the river.

Irvine said she first noticed the oily substance leaving a rainbow film on the river's surface and a strong acrid smell in early 2025.

She reported it to the EA in July that year when she believed it was bubbling up rather than coming from boats.

The EA first dismissed the substance as surface run-off but, after Irvine continued sending photos, including of dead wildlife, the investigation reopened in May this year.

"This stretch of the Avon used to regularly have 30 to 40 ducks, but now it's unusual to see more than a handful," she said.

"I have personally found dead fish, ducks and ducklings. I know we can't prove it, but there has to be a link with the pollution."

The EA's investigations so far suggest a likely cause is contamination linked to pollution from the former tar works that operated in the area from the mid 19th Century up to the 1980s, but further work is needed.

Irvine said the issue had been even worse during this summer's heatwaves, which had led to her being prescribed medication for migraines.

"It would all bubble up, the smell would be so strong, it would surround the whole house," she said.

The EA said the pollution was a category three pollution incident because impacts were limited to the area where contamination enters the watercourse.

"I cant believe that even with all the health concerns and the fact there are otters in this river as well, it's still deemed minor," Irvine said.

In 2022, a leaked internal EA report told staff to ignore lower-impact category three and four pollution reports because of limited funding to investigate.

"I've been so frustrated with the EA," Irvine said. "It feels like pulling teeth trying to get any action from them."

The EA is also investigating another incident nearby at Brislington Brook , where dead fish and eels, foam on the water and "an intense chemical smell" were reported by volunteers.

Dominic Linnell, who walks his dog along the river every day, said he first noticed the issue more than two years ago.

"Two or three times a week, there's an awful chemical smell, and I see a huge oil slick that seems to bubble up from the bottom of the river," he said.

"I've seen fish floating dead and ducks. There's a lot of wildlife along there, you get herons, so it's a real shame.

"We all really care about the river, it's definitely killing wildlife and it's very unpleasant," he said.

Another local resident, Tristan Dhalla, said he had noticed the pollution ever since he moved to the area five years ago, and neighbours had even claimed the problem went back as far as a decade.

Wessex Water said their investigation had found "no issues" with any of their assets, while the substance did not pass through their sewerage network.

A Bristol City Council spokesperson said it was supporting the EA's investigation by providing information and records, while officers had visited the site last week.

articles.title: Russian strikes kill eight, injure dozens across Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukrainian leader Zelenskyy says Moscow launched nearly 4,000 drones, aerial bombs and missiles on Ukraine in past week.
articles.body:
A Russian military strike on northeastern Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, has injured at least 22 people, including children, less than a day after eight people were killed in attacks nationwide.

Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekov said on his Telegram account that a guided Russian aerial bomb hit an apartment block early on Monday, destroying two floors of the multistorey building.

He said six children were among the injured.

Russian attacks were also reported across Ukraine on Sunday.

Ukrainian Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said three people, including a 16-year-old girl, were killed in air strikes that damaged a children’s centre in the northern city of Sumy.

Authorities in the Odesa region, meanwhile, said a “massive strike” on the south of the Black Sea region killed one person and damaged residential buildings, a shop, a hotel, a medical building, and a grain warehouse.

And in the capital, Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a woman and two 16-year-olds were injured and hospitalised.

“The enemy continues to relentlessly attack the Kyiv region with strike drones,” the city’s administration said.

“Sixteen sites have been damaged”, including 12 houses, a warehouse and a production facility, it added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that three people were killed in strikes in the southern Zaporizhia region and that a Russian drone strike had killed one man in Kyiv.

Zelenskyy said in a post on his X account that Russia had launched more than 2,200 attack drones, 1,630 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types against Ukraine in the past week.

“If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps towards de-escalation, as it claims, particularly to American negotiators, this wave of Shahed terror would not be happening,” Zelenskyy said in later comments, referring to the Iran-developed drones Moscow has used against Ukraine.

In Moscow, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it had bombed a Kyivstar data centre in Kyiv and another belonging to the Omega Telecom company. It said that the firms were providing services to the Ukrainian army.

Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov told the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Saturday that Moscow intended to continue its military campaign “to the end”.

Ukrainian drones struck an oil depot in Russia’s Krasnodar region on Monday, according to local reports.

Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ published footage of a large fire and identified the facility as the Pavlovskaya oil depot.

Ukraine has intensified its targeting of Russian oil infrastructure in recent weeks.

United States-led talks to end the war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, have failed to produce a breakthrough, and the UN has highlighted the growing civilian toll.

articles.title: Jersey's redeveloped airport departure lounge to open in November
articles.summary: The first phase of the project from Jersey Ports will include new seating and work spaces.
articles.body:
The first phase of a project to redevelop Jersey Airport's departure lounge is due to open to the public in early November.

The work forms part of a £10m project by Ports of Jersey to modernise the airport , improve passenger facilities and replace ageing infrastructure.

Project leaders said the new lounge would include an improved layout, expanded seating areas and a new mezzanine level with runway views.

Ports chief executive Matt Thomas said the changes would "massively enhance the experience" for passengers.

The first stage of project had been developed with input from charities, businesses and tourism, heritage, arts and passenger groups, project leaders said.

Features would include wicker Jersey cows, aerial images of the island, a Martello-inspired lift tower and a Plémont Bay-themed family area, they added.

Thomas said the project was also making changes to the ageing infrastructure of the airport.

He said: "This project is about much more than creating a beautiful space for our passengers.

"Substantial investment has been made in the 30-year-old infrastructure that supports the airport's long-term future, including improvements to heating, ventilation and other essential systems."

The next phase of the project was due to open in 2027 and included an enhanced food and drink area, larger assisted travel lounge, refurbished main toilet facilities and a shop dedicated to Jersey produce, project bosses said.

articles.title: Carer at home investigated by BBC struck off for threatening elderly man
articles.summary: Amina Sani, who is Nigerian, was found to have threatened the 81-year-old with police and threatened to hit him.
articles.body:
A carer who was secretly filmed mocking and threatening an elderly bedbound man with dementia has been struck off.

Amina Sani was found to have threatened the 81-year-old with police and threatened to hit him when he became distressed and lashed out at the prospect of being showered against his will.

The Nigerian worker went on to carry out the man's intimate personal care while a cleaner held his arms down.

The incidents at Castlehill Care Home in Inverness on 10 April last year came to light after the resident's daughter installed a secret camera in his room due to concerns over his care.

The footage was later featured in a BBC documentary into care standards at Castlehill, in which families accused the home of "cruelty" and "neglect".

Sani's legal representative told a Scottish Social Services Council misconduct hearing that she had not been trained properly in what was her first job in the UK.

Worker at care home in BBC investigation faces being struck off

Care home in BBC probe making progress on improvements, says watchdog

I went undercover as a cleaner at a failing care home. Here's what I witnessed

Namatirai Chipere said her client was a victim of problems in the social care system herself.

However, hearing chairman Iain Burke said the incidents were a "significant abuse of trust and power" for which she had shown no insight or remorse.

He said her attitude and behaviour were "fundamentally incompatible" with registration as a social care worker.

In a statement, the home's owner - Morar Living - said it acted promptly when concerns were brought to its attention.

It said there was "no truth" in Sani's claim that she was not trained properly.

Castlehill, now renamed Morar Highland, was graded "good" in its most recent care inspection.

The panel was shown video footage covering a period of more than 20 minutes, in which Sani repeatedly tells the bed man that he was to be showered. He can be heard screaming "no" and "leave me alone", before swearing at Sani and another carer.

The pair can be seen laughing during the encounter.

During evidence at the hearing, the man's daughter Su Christie, said her father, a former merchant navy crewman, had a lifelong fear of showers due to a childhood trauma.

Following the judgement, she said: "You could tell by the things he was doing, the things he was saying, that his distress was growing and growing throughout that interaction and there was no attempt to bring him down or de-escalate him whatsoever.

"He didn't know what was going on. He's a confused 81-year-old man living with dementia. He was frightened.

"It was devastating, utterly devastating. I was in shock because, although I knew there were issues, I didn't expect to see that. It was very distressing to watch."

The panel ruled Sani told Christie's father: "We will call the police and they will take you to court" and, referring to a male cleaner, "do you think that man is going to hit you?" or words to that effect.

She also pulled his duvet off without any warning, causing him to become distressed and agitated.

Delivering the panel's judgment, the chairman said: "We agree with your solicitor's submissions that you were let down by your employer, and there is little doubt that there was institutional failure.

"None of the failures you have highlighted absolve you from your personal responsibility as a registered social care worker."

"It is clear throughout the video clips that you did not show any kindness or compassion to the resident. At one point you and your colleague can be seen laughing in response to something the resident says or does.

"It does not appear to us to be laughing with the resident, but it appears more disrespectful in nature. We find that the resident suffered harm and you did not respect his dignity."

Burke added that the panel felt Sani's treatment of the man was "not something that could be remediated with training" as it reflected her attitude.

It also noted she failed to use any de-escalation techniques.

In closing submissions, Sani's legal representative said her client wished to apologise to the family.

Christie, who moved her father into a new home shortly after the incident, said: "I think it was the right decision.

"Whilst the panel did comment on institutional failures, this hearing is about her own personal accountability. And I think it sends the message that personal accountability matters.

"In a care setting, people living this dementia, like my father, should be treated with respect, dignity, and patience and courtesy. They should be treated as human beings and that's all I was asking for."

A hearing to decide sanctions over the behaviour of carer Oluwabunmi Salami, involving the same man, continues.

Earlier in the hearing, Salami admitted allegations that she raised and lowered the man's bed without warning, causing him distress.

A spokesperson for Morar Living said: "There is no truth in Amina Sani's claim that she was not trained properly by Morar.

"When concerns were brought to our attention, Morar Highland acted promptly, including suspending employees where appropriate, undertaking formal investigations and taking action in line with the findings.

"We made the relevant referrals to the Scottish Social Services Council (SSSC) and, where required, to the Protecting Vulnerable Groups (PVG) Scheme.

"The safety, dignity and wellbeing of our residents remains our priority, and all concerns regarding staff conduct are taken seriously and acted upon appropriately."
